title: 2.345 rounds UP to 2.35 while 1.005 rounds DOWN to 1.00 - same "x.xx5" shape, opposite outcome
assumption: Any price ending in exactly half a cent (x.xx5) rounds the same way - either always up, or always down.

input.description: Two different prices that both look like a clean half-cent boundary, rounded to cents for display.

what_goes_wrong: 2.345 rounds to "2.35" (up) but 1.005 rounds to "1.00" (down), even though both are written with the same "value.value5" shape - there is no way to predict which direction a given half-cent literal will round without checking its actual binary value.
why: Neither 2.345 nor 1.005 is exactly representable in IEEE-754 double. 2.345's nearest double happens to be a hair above 2.345 (2.34500000000000019540...), so it's not actually a tie and rounds up; 1.005's nearest double happens to be a hair below 1.005 (1.00499999999999989341...), so it rounds down. Both languages round the true stored binary value, not the decimal text you typed, and whether a given literal lands slightly above or below its decimal value is essentially unpredictable without inspecting the bits.
affects: any IEEE-754 double formatted by rounding its true binary value
fix: Never treat float literals as exact decimal values for money. Round and store amounts as integer minor units, or construct a Decimal from the original decimal string (not from a float), so rounding operates on the number you actually meant.

sources.title: Python docs: 15.1. Floating-Point Arithmetic: Issues and Limitations

test_cases.note: A money-rounding function that takes the exact decimal string "1.005" and rounds half-cents up should return "1.01" - if it instead parses to a float first and formats with toFixed, it will silently return "1.00".
